title: House and Cellar
premise: Edmund Dunmore, a hospice nurse who has spent twelve years hearing the dying count backwards toward zero, returns to her childhood village of Marrow Fen to settle her late mother's house. On her first night, the church bell that was melted down in 1911 rings thirteen times, and the whole village falls asleep except those the bell has chosen. Edmund discovers that in 1911 the villagers sold their dead's memories to something beneath the cellar of the old rectory, buying themselves prosperity — and now it has come to collect a century of interest. To survive until sunrise and free the village, Edmund must descend into the cellar, offer it her own most precious memory instead, and learn that belonging was always the price being purchased.
about_author: Hazel Okonkwo is a former palliative care volunteer from the Norfolk fens who writes horror about the quiet bargains ordinary people make. House and Cellar is her third novel, following the critically acclaimed The Tallyman's Daughter.

chapters.title: The Counting Ward
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. In her hospice ward, a dying man counts backwards from thirty and stops at zero with a smile of pure terror. Edmund tells herself, as she has for twelve years, that it's coincidence. Emotional beat: weary denial established; the reader sees what she refuses to.

chapters.title: Marrow Fen
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. She drives back to her inherited childhood house, noting the village's unnatural prosperity — no poverty, no graves newer than 1911. Old Mrs. Achebe warns her not to stay past dark. Emotional beat: homecoming laced with wrongness; belonging feels like a trap already sprung.

chapters.title: Thirteen Strokes
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. At midnight the melted-down church bell rings thirteen times. Every light in the village dies at once. Her phone shows no signal; the road out loops back on itself. Emotional beat: denial shatters; dread becomes physical.

chapters.title: The Sleeping Village
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. She finds every villager asleep mid-motion — dinner half-eaten, cars idling — except the vicar, Reverend Sloane, who is awake and weeping. He says only: 'It rang for you.' Emotional beat: isolation sharpens into guilt.

chapters.title: What Mother Kept
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV, with a letter from her mother in italics. In the house she finds her mother's research: parish records showing the entire village died in the winter of 1911 and were 'restored' by something in the rectory cellar. Emotional beat: grief curdles into betrayal — her mother knew and stayed silent.

chapters.title: The Bargain of 1911
chapters.summary: Sloane's POV. Flashback through his predecessor's diary: starving villagers traded their dead's memories to the thing below for life and luck, renewing the debt each generation. This generation's payment fell due tonight. Emotional beat: complicity across generations; power corrupting a desperate community.

chapters.title: Chosen by the Bell
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. Sloane explains why she alone is awake: the thing remembers her — as a child she wandered into the cellar and it tasted her memory and let her go, keeping a claim. Emotional beat: the horror of being marked; childhood nostalgia reinterpreted as predation.

chapters.title: Voices in the Walls
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. The sleeping villagers begin sleepwalking toward the rectory, murmuring fragments of memories they no longer own. Edmund recognizes her mother's voice among them, counting backwards. Emotional beat: heartbreak; the counting motif turns intimate.

chapters.title: The Vicar's Confession
chapters.summary: Sloane's POV. He admits he renewed the bargain twenty years ago to save his dying daughter, spending other people's memories as currency. His daughter sleeps and does not know him anymore. Emotional beat: sympathy for a corrupted man; power's cost made personal.

chapters.title: Zero Hour
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. The last sleeper reaches zero and dissolves into grey dust that drifts toward the rectory. Dawn is four hours away, but time inside the fen moves differently — the clock runs backwards. Emotional beat: urgency inverted; hope begins to feel like a trick.

chapters.title: The Rectory Door
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. She and Sloane reach the rectory; the door opens before they knock. Inside, wallpapered halls display framed photographs of moments stolen from villagers' lives. One frame holds Edmund's own eighth birthday. Emotional beat: violation of the self; memory as property.

chapters.title: Down the Cellar Stairs
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. The stairs descend farther than the house is deep. Warm air smells of loam and candlewax. Sloane falters at the threshold, unable to enter — only the claimed may approach. Edmund goes down alone. Emotional beat: courage born of having nothing left to lose.

chapters.title: The Tenant Below
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. In the cellar sits a patient, courteous presence wearing the accumulated faces of everyone it has fed on, speaking in the voices of the dying she has nursed. It offers her a seat at its table. Emotional beat: seduction; the monster is almost kind, which is worse.

chapters.title: An Accounting
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. The creature itemizes the village's century of purchases — harvests, health, her mother's remission — and presents the bill: one hundred years of memories, or one soul freely given. Emotional beat: the banality of evil as bookkeeping; power dressed as contract.

chapters.title: What Edmund Remembers
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV, intercut with sensory flashbacks. Forced to review her life as collateral, she realizes her happiest memories are ones she can't verify — some were sold to her mother to buy comfort. Emotional beat: identity destabilized; memory revealed as unreliable currency.

chapters.title: The Counter-Offer
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. Instead of surrendering, she offers a trade the thing cannot refuse: twelve years of hearing the dying count — she knows exactly when each sleeper hits zero, and she will teach it to wait, to savor, if it releases the village. Emotional beat: agency reclaimed; turning her curse into leverage.

chapters.title: The Thing That Waits
chapters.summary: The creature's POV, brief and alien. It has never been offered patience — only fear and hunger. Intrigued, it tests her sincerity by letting her feel a century of borrowed memories at once. Emotional beat: vertigo; empathy extended even to the monstrous.

chapters.title: Sunrise Terms
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. As dawn greys the cellar, they strike terms: the villagers wake with their memories returned minus one small moment each; Edmund stays as the fen's keeper, renewing the bargain honestly, year by year, face to face. Emotional beat: bittersweet resolution; belonging accepted at last, on her terms.

chapters.title: Waking
chapters.summary: Village ensemble POV, rotating briefly. The villagers wake confused, missing small things — a first kiss, a favorite song — and find themselves strangely kinder for the gaps. Sloane's daughter remembers him. Emotional beat: communal grace; loss transmuted into connection.

chapters.title: The Keeper of Marrow Fen
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. Weeks later, she takes the hospice job at the fen's edge, tending the village's dying herself so the counting happens under her watch. The bell tower stands empty, but sometimes at dusk she hears a single soft note, like acknowledgment. Emotional beat: peace without closure; duty embraced.

chapters.title: A New Tenant
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. A stranger arrives asking about houses for sale, and Edmund recognizes the hungry look she once wore — someone else has heard the counting elsewhere. She invites them to tea, beginning the long work of teaching the thing below restraint. Emotional beat: vigilance; the cycle acknowledged but tended.

chapters.title: House and Cellar
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV, final night. She descends the cellar stairs with two cups of tea and reads aloud to the darkness from her mother's letters, giving it memories freely rather than letting it take. Above, the village sleeps soundly, counting nothing. Emotional beat: quiet transcendence; belonging chosen, not bought.
